## Not "how many" but "how long until"

Most epidemiological headlines count cases. But some of the most important
questions are about *timing*: how long until a newly established mosquito
population produces its first local outbreak? How long until a region crosses a
risk threshold? **Time-to-event analysis** (a.k.a. survival analysis) is built
exactly for these "how long until" questions — including cases where the event
hasn't happened yet (censoring).

## The core ideas, briefly

- **The event and the clock.** Define the event (e.g. first local outbreak) and
  when the clock starts (e.g. vector establishment).
- **Censoring.** Regions that haven't had an outbreak by the end of follow-up still
  carry information — survival methods use it instead of discarding it.
- **The survival curve.** Kaplan–Meier curves show the probability of remaining
  event-free over time; hazard models (e.g. Cox) quantify what speeds the clock up.

## What it revealed for Europe

Applying these methods to dengue and chikungunya, the interval between
*Aedes albopictus* establishing in a European region and its first local outbreak
**fell from around 25 years to under five** over 1990–2024 — with a projected
near five-fold increase in outbreaks by the 2060s under a high-emissions scenario.

preparedness.)*

## Try it yourself

The same tools underpin my [Survival Analysis project](../../../Celiac.html), which
walks through Kaplan–Meier and Cox models in R on a clinical dataset. The full
outbreak study is in
[*The Lancet Planetary Health*](https://doi.org/10.1016/S2542-5196(25)00059-2).
